questions.stem: Which is a positive economic impact of tourism on a host region?
options: crowding of local beaches during school holidays
the revival of traditional crafts and dances
erosion of walking tracks in a national park
jobs in accommodation, food and tour services
questions.explanation: Employment and income from tourist spending are economic impacts. Crowding is a social impact, craft revival a cultural impact and track erosion an environmental impact.

questions.stem: In tourism geography, economic leakage refers to:
options: the extra local spending that follows when tourism workers' wages are spent in nearby shops
the gradual loss of a culture's traditions through contact with tourists
the number of visitors a site can hold before it is damaged
tourist spending that flows out of the host area, such as to foreign owners
questions.explanation: Leakage occurs when profits go to overseas owners or money is spent on imported goods and staff, so it does not stay in the local economy. Extra local spending from tourism wages is the multiplier effect.

questions.stem: A tourist pays a local guide, who spends part of her wages at the town's bakery, whose owner then buys from a local farm. This chain is called:
options: economic leakage
the demonstration effect
carrying capacity
the multiplier effect
questions.explanation: The multiplier effect is the way tourist spending circulates through a local economy, creating further income and jobs. Leakage is the opposite, where money leaves the area.

questions.stem: On a small island, most resorts are foreign-owned, much of the food is imported and senior managers come from overseas. Compared with locally owned guesthouses, these resorts are likely to:
options: create no jobs at all for people who live on the island
remove the need for any imported goods on the island
keep a smaller share of tourist spending in the island's economy
keep a larger share of tourist spending in the island's own local economy
questions.explanation: Foreign ownership, imports and expatriate staff increase leakage, so less of each dollar stays locally. The resorts still employ some islanders, so they do create jobs.

questions.stem: Many jobs at Victoria's alpine resorts are available only in the snow season. An economic issue this creates is:
options: a permanent shortage of visitors during the winter
the loss of all natural snow cover in the high country
an end to all tourism businesses in nearby valley towns
unstable year-round employment and income for workers
questions.explanation: Seasonality concentrates income in a few months, so workers and businesses face uneven earnings. Resorts respond by promoting summer activities to spread visitation across the year.

questions.stem: Cruise passengers visiting a port for a single day often spend relatively little in the local economy because:
options: their meals and accommodation are already provided on the ship
they are not allowed to leave the ship at any port of call on the voyage
they are domestic tourists who do not use foreign currency
all port towns ban cruise passengers from local businesses
questions.explanation: Most cruise spending goes to the cruise company, so ports gain mainly from short-stay purchases and tours. This is a form of leakage that limits the economic benefit to host towns.

questions.stem: In some popular coastal towns, many houses are listed as short-stay holiday rentals. A social issue this can create is:
options: lower demand for accommodation from visiting tourists in the summer months
an increase in the town's permanent population every year
a fall in the number of tourism jobs available in the town
less long-term rental housing for local workers and rising rents
questions.explanation: When homes are rented to visitors instead of residents, local workers struggle to find affordable housing. Some councils and state governments have responded with levies or limits on short-stay rentals.

questions.stem: When a traditional ceremony is shortened and staged on a timetable for paying tourists, this is described as:
options: economic leakage
the demonstration effect on residents
the commodification of culture
the multiplier effect
questions.explanation: Commodification turns cultural practices into products for sale, which can strip them of meaning. It is a negative cultural impact, though careful management can also help keep traditions alive.

questions.stem: Young people in a remote host community begin copying the clothing, spending and habits of visiting tourists. This is an example of:
options: commodification of the local landscape
acculturation through the demonstration effect
the multiplier effect of tourist spending
economic leakage to foreign-owned firms
questions.explanation: The demonstration effect occurs when locals imitate visitors' behaviour, which can lead to acculturation, the loss or change of local culture through contact. Commodification refers to turning culture into a product for sale.

questions.stem: Which is a positive cultural impact of tourism?
options: traffic congestion on the main road into a town
loss of farmland to the building of new resorts and golf courses
rising local house prices during the peak season
demand from visitors that helps revive traditional crafts
questions.explanation: Tourist interest can give communities a reason and income to keep crafts, music and languages alive. The other effects are social, environmental or economic impacts, and they are negative.

questions.stem: In Doxey's Irridex, residents who openly blame tourists for local problems and protest against them are at which stage?
options: apathy
annoyance
antagonism
euphoria
questions.explanation: The Irridex runs from euphoria to apathy to annoyance and finally antagonism as tourism grows. Annoyance involves irritation and concern, but open hostility marks antagonism.

questions.stem: A geographer surveys residents of a beach town at the start and end of the summer. Over the season, the share saying tourists 'make the town worse' rises from 10% to 45%. This best shows that:
options: tourist numbers in the town must have fallen during the summer
the town has passed the stagnation stage of the life cycle
social impacts of tourism can change over a short temporal scale
the town's permanent resident population fell by 35% during the summer
questions.explanation: The survey measures residents' attitudes, which shifted as the season progressed, showing a change over time. The figures are percentages of respondents, not changes in population or visitor numbers.

questions.stem: Which management strategy most directly reduces trampling damage on a popular walking track?
options: allowing visitors to choose their own routes
building raised boardwalks and hardened paths
advertising the track to attract more visitors
removing signs that mark the edges of the track
questions.explanation: Boardwalks and hardened surfaces keep feet off fragile soils and plants and concentrate use on a durable surface. Spreading visitors across unmarked routes would widen the damage.

questions.stem: A transect from a car park to a lookout shows bare soil and exposed roots near the car park and track, and dense ground cover 50 m away. The most likely explanation is that:
options: trampling is concentrated where visitor numbers are greatest
plants grow best close to the car park because of the shade
the soil far from the track has been eroded the most by visitors
ground cover is unrelated to the distribution of visitors
questions.explanation: The pattern of damage matches the pattern of use, a spatial association between visitors and trampling. A transect is a useful fieldwork tool for showing this change over distance.

questions.stem: To measure trampling impact at a tourist site during fieldwork, a student could:
options: survey visitors about which country they come from and why
look up the site's average rainfall online
compare plant cover in quadrats on and beside the track
count the cars in the car park on one morning
questions.explanation: Quadrats give primary data on plant cover, and comparing used and unused areas isolates the effect of trampling. Car counts and origin surveys measure visitor numbers and types, not environmental impact.

questions.stem: The maximum number of visitors a site can support without unacceptable damage to its environment or to the visitor experience is its:
options: relative distance
multiplier effect
economic leakage
carrying capacity
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity sets a limit on use, which managers apply through quotas, permits and timed tickets. It can be physical, environmental or social, depending on what is being protected.

questions.stem: The UNWTO defines sustainable tourism as tourism that:
options: takes full account of its current and future economic, social and environmental impacts
grows visitor numbers every year, regardless of the effect on host communities and environments
takes place only in natural areas, with no buildings or infrastructure
is run by governments rather than by any private tourism businesses
questions.explanation: Sustainable tourism addresses the needs of visitors, industry, the environment and host communities, now and into the future. It can take place in cities and be run by private businesses.

questions.stem: A resort is profitable and employs many locals, but it drained a coastal wetland to build its golf course. In terms of sustainability, the resort is:
options: environmentally sustainable but economically unsustainable
sustainable in every way, because it provides local jobs
socially unsustainable, because it employs local people
economically beneficial but environmentally unsustainable
questions.explanation: Sustainability has economic, social, cultural and environmental dimensions, and a project can score well on one and poorly on another. Destroying a wetland harms environmental sustainability even if jobs are created.

questions.stem: Mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef is caused mainly by:
options: fresh water from rivers raising the salt content of the sea
prolonged high sea temperatures that make corals expel their algae
tourists touching and standing on the coral while snorkelling on popular reefs
cold winter currents flowing north from the Southern Ocean
questions.explanation: Marine heatwaves linked to climate change cause corals to expel the algae that give them colour and food. Touching coral causes local damage, but mass bleaching over huge areas is driven by heat.

questions.stem: Most of the greenhouse gas emissions caused by tourism come from:
options: guided walks in national parks
transport, especially air travel
hotel laundries and swimming pools
souvenirs made in the host country
questions.explanation: Studies for the UNWTO have found transport to be the largest source of tourism emissions, with aviation a major share. This links tourism to climate change, which in turn threatens destinations such as reefs and ski fields.

questions.stem: With shorter, less reliable snow seasons, Victoria's alpine resorts have expanded snowmaking and promoted summer mountain biking. A key limitation of relying on snowmaking is that it:
options: makes the climate across the alpine region colder for the season
needs cold enough temperatures, plus large amounts of water and energy
works only when natural snow is already falling heavily at the resort
removes the need for resorts to attract visitors in other seasons
questions.explanation: Snowmaking machines need cold, dry conditions, so warmer winters limit the days they can run, and they use a lot of water and electricity. Promoting summer activities spreads risk across the year.

questions.stem: Rising sea levels threaten low-lying island destinations such as the Maldives, while tourist flights to them add to greenhouse emissions. This illustrates that:
options: island tourism has no interconnection with global climate
tourism both contributes to climate change and is threatened by it
climate change affects tourism only in cold, alpine destinations
tourist flights lower sea levels around the islands they visit
questions.explanation: Tourism is interconnected with climate change at a global scale: travel releases emissions, and the resulting changes threaten the attractions that draw visitors. This is a key challenge for sustainable tourism.

questions.stem: Before approving a new resort next to a national park, planners require an environmental impact assessment. Its main purpose is to:
options: identify likely impacts and conditions to reduce them before approval
advertise the new resort to overseas visitors before it opens
set the room prices that the resort is allowed to charge its guests in peak season
guarantee that the resort will make a profit in its first year
questions.explanation: Planning tools such as impact assessments let governments refuse projects or attach conditions before damage occurs. This is cheaper and more effective than repairing harm afterwards.

questions.stem: In 1985 the Victorian Government began buying back houses in the Summerland Peninsula estate on Phillip Island and removing them, restoring little penguin habitat near the Penguin Parade. This strategy is an example of:
options: a quota that limits the number of visitors to the island
planning that removed development to protect a key tourist attraction
economic leakage of tourism profits to overseas owners of the island's resorts
acculturation of residents through contact with visitors
questions.explanation: Removing houses and roads from the penguins' breeding area reduced threats such as cars and pets, protecting the wildlife that draws visitors. It shows long-term planning trading short-term costs for sustainability.

questions.stem: Peru limits the number of permits issued each day to walk the Inca Trail to Machu Picchu. This strategy mainly:
options: removes the need for guides on the trail
lets any visitor walk without a booking
keeps use within the trail's carrying capacity
increases the number of walkers each year
questions.explanation: Daily permit quotas limit crowding, erosion and waste on the trail. Walkers must book through licensed operators, so the strategy also supports local guides and porters.

questions.stem: In the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park zoning plan, green zones (Marine National Park Zones) are areas where:
options: commercial fishing is allowed, but recreational fishing is banned
resorts may be built on the reef, provided they pay a fee
fishing and collecting are banned, but activities such as snorkelling are allowed
all visitors are banned, including tourists on private boats, snorkellers and scuba divers
questions.explanation: Green zones are 'no-take' areas: nothing may be removed, but people may visit, swim, snorkel and dive. Zoning separates conflicting uses so the reef can be used and conserved at the same time.

questions.stem: The Environmental Management Charge paid by visitors on commercial Great Barrier Reef tours is used to:
options: pay the wages of tour boat crews and guides
buy fuel for the tour operators' boats
fund advertising for overseas reef holidays
help fund the management of the Marine Park
questions.explanation: The charge is collected by operators and passed to the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority for management, research and education. It links visitor use to the cost of protecting the reef.

questions.stem: Venice has trialled an entry fee for day-trippers on peak days. To evaluate whether the fee reduced overcrowding, a geographer should mainly compare:
options: the total revenue the city collected from the fee in its first season
the number of hotel rooms in Venice before and after the fee began
the opinions of tourists who had never visited Venice before the fee
visitor numbers and crowding on fee days with similar days without the fee
questions.explanation: The fee's aim was to reduce crowding, so its effectiveness is judged by changes in crowding against a fair comparison. Revenue shows how much money was raised, not whether crowding fell.

questions.stem: Large cruise ships are no longer allowed to sail through Venice's Giudecca Canal past St Mark's Square. Which impacts was this measure mainly aimed at reducing?
options: the commodification of rowing races on the Grand Canal
the falling number of day-trippers arriving in the city
damage to the lagoon and old buildings, pollution and crowding
economic leakage from the city's locally owned restaurants
questions.explanation: Huge ships caused wash that eroded foundations, added air and water pollution, and landed large crowds in the historic centre. The measure responded to environmental and social impacts of overtourism.

questions.stem: The climb at Uluru was permanently closed in October 2019. The main reason given by the Anangu traditional owners was that:
options: the rock had become unstable and was likely to collapse onto walkers soon
visitor numbers to the national park had fallen to almost none
a new resort was planned for the summit of the rock itself
the climb follows a sacred route and climbing disrespects Tjukurpa
questions.explanation: Anangu had long asked visitors not to climb because the route has deep cultural significance under Tjukurpa, their traditional law. The closure is a management response to a cultural impact that also improves safety.

questions.stem: Galápagos National Park requires visitors to stay on marked trails and to be accompanied by licensed naturalist guides. This strategy mainly reduces:
options: the number of cruise ships visiting the Caribbean
the cultural distance between visitors and guides
disturbance to wildlife and damage to fragile habitats
economic leakage from Ecuador's locally owned hotels
questions.explanation: Trails and guides control where visitors go and how close they get to animals, while guides also educate visitors. Licensed guiding also creates local jobs, supporting economic sustainability.

questions.stem: Asking visitors to cover their shoulders and knees when entering temples is a strategy mainly aimed at reducing:
options: cultural offence to the host community
environmental damage to temple gardens
economic leakage from temple entry fees
crowding at the temple's car park
questions.explanation: Codes of conduct and dress codes help visitors respect local religious and cultural norms. They address cultural impacts, which are part of ethical tourism.

questions.stem: Community-based tourism, such as village homestays run by local families, is valued in ethical tourism mainly because it:
options: removes all contact between visitors and local families
keeps control and benefits of tourism with local people
sends most tourist spending to international companies
replaces local culture with visitors' customs and habits
questions.explanation: When communities own and run tourism, more income stays local and residents decide how their culture and land are shared. This reduces leakage and supports social and cultural sustainability.

questions.stem: Ecotourism Australia's ECO Certification helps travellers to choose tourism operators that:
options: are owned by the Australian or state governments
have the most visitors of any business in their area
meet standards for sustainable and responsible practice
offer the cheapest prices in each tourism region
questions.explanation: Certification assesses operators against criteria such as environmental management, interpretation and community benefit. It gives travellers a way to identify ethical and sustainable businesses.

questions.stem: A limitation of voluntary tourism certification schemes as a management strategy is that:
options: they guarantee visitors lower prices than other operators
they measure only the profits made by each operator
operators who choose not to join are not assessed at all
they ban uncertified operators from every national park
questions.explanation: Because joining is optional, many operators are never assessed, and travellers may not check for the label. Certification improves practice among members but does not cover the whole industry.

questions.stem: Which indicator would best show whether a daily visitor quota has reduced environmental damage at a site?
options: the number of tourism websites that mention the site each year
the change in vegetation cover at the site before and after the quota
the number of visitors who said they enjoyed their visit to the site that year
the price of a ticket to enter the site before and after the quota
questions.explanation: An environmental goal needs an environmental measure, such as vegetation cover, soil erosion or wildlife counts, compared before and after the strategy. Visitor enjoyment and ticket prices measure other things.

questions.stem: A national park raises its entry fee sharply to reduce crowding. An issue this creates for social sustainability is that the fee:
options: increases crowding by attracting more visitors to the park
reduces the park's income available for management
removes all environmental protection from the park
can price out lower-income visitors, including local residents
questions.explanation: Price-based strategies can work against equity, because they ration access by ability to pay. Some parks respond with discounts for locals or free days, showing the trade-offs in management.

questions.stem: The Twelve Apostles have a visitor centre, sealed paths and viewing platforms set back from the cliff edge. Which evaluation of this strategy is most accurate?
options: it has increased damage, because visitors now walk freely over all the cliff tops
it has no effect on visitors, because the platforms are built away from the coast
it protects fragile cliff tops by concentrating visitors, but cannot stop natural coastal erosion
it stops the limestone stacks from eroding any further, so they will now remain unchanged indefinitely
questions.explanation: Paths and platforms channel large numbers of visitors onto hard surfaces and away from unstable edges, reducing human impact and risk. The stacks are formed and destroyed by wave erosion, which management cannot halt.

questions.stem: A tourist town wants to reduce the economic leakage from its visitor spending. Which strategy would be most effective?
options: inviting a foreign hotel chain to build a large all-inclusive resort on the beach
importing most food and souvenirs so that visitors pay lower prices
hiring senior staff from overseas instead of training local people
supporting locally owned businesses and local suppliers of food and goods
questions.explanation: Leakage falls when ownership, supplies and jobs are local, so more spending circulates through the multiplier effect. All-inclusive resorts, imports and expatriate staff all increase leakage.

questions.stem: A coastal town's tourism brings jobs, but residents complain of crowding and rising rents, and dunes are eroding. A council plan that would best address all three dimensions of sustainability is:
options: banning all tourism from the town to remove every impact on residents
removing dune vegetation to widen the beach for larger summer crowds
capping short-stay rentals, fencing dunes and holding off-peak events
doubling peak-season marketing, building more car parks along the dunes and approving new resorts
questions.explanation: Housing limits address social impacts, dune protection addresses environmental impacts, and off-peak events spread economic benefits across the year. Banning tourism would end the jobs, so it fails economic sustainability.
